scope: The late operating Lyttelton Gaol around 1903. Includes the Oxford Street entrance and connected frontage, masonry perimeter, cell ranges on two main terraced yards, and subordinate service courts. The separate Warder’s House across Oxford Street, interiors and later Upham clock are outside scope.

primaryWrittenSources.facts: The gaol closed in 1920. The main buildings were demolished in 1922–24. The listing retains the former site and surviving early concrete structures.
The National Library identifies an archival copy negative of Plate 1 from C. E. Matthews’s government-printed 1923 book.
The 1878 Gaols Committee describes new concrete wings, older wood and iron portions, separate yards and 185 cells in the general prison description.
A contemporary public works account describes concrete construction with separate stone dressing and carpentry at the gaol.
The 1873 Lyttelton Times report describes approximately 10-foot floor-to-ceiling cell rooms in the new Mountfort work.
